I made a really sweet picture, I don’t want to post it here because it’s personal, but it was a picture of my mom smiling and holding my younger brother, as my dad pushed me on the swing in the background. My mom also hasn’t hung the picture up which really hurts my feelings. AITA?

It took me like 6 weeks or so to finish this painting. I gave it to my mom, and she cried she loved it. My parents aren’t together anymore but they were good friends until my mom met my step dad. First thing he said when she opened the painting was, “well, where am I?” This pissed me off and I ignored it but he kept going, saying if I needed a reference picture I could have asked him, and calling me rude and “exclusionary” because he’s a part of the family too and kept going on and on. I told him I didn’t paint him because I can’t stand to look at his face for that long. He slammed the table like a petulant child and stormed out. My mom scolded me for being rude, and asked me to apologize for not putting him in the painting. WHAT? I still haven’t said a word to this man, it’s been about three weeks. My mom also hasn’t hung the picture up which really hurts my feelings. AITA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **0 (Not the asshole)** **Here's why:** - **The painting was a specific, personal memory** of *your biological family unit* (you, your mom, and your biological dad) during a time *before* your stepfather entered the picture. It was never intended to be a " family" portrait inclusive of everyone in the current household. - **Stepfather has no claim to be in it**. He wasn't part of that moment, and his demand to be included (especially after the fact) is entitled and inappropriate. His "exclusionary" accusation is nonsensical—you didn't exclude him from a group photo; you created a *private, nostalgic artwork* about a time he wasn't in your life. - **Your boundary is valid**. "I can't stand to look at his face for that long" is a clear emotional boundary. No one should be forced to include someone they're uncomfortable with in their art, especially when it's a deeply personal gift for their * biological* parent. - **Stepfather's behavior was the real issue**. Slamming the table, calling you "rude," and demanding an apology for a boundary he violated is immature and toxic. *He* is the one acting like the "asshole" here. - **Your mom's reaction is concerning** (she should support *your* boundaries, not stepfather's entitlement), but ** that doesn't make * you* wrong**. Her choice not to hang the painting is her own issue to work through—not a reflection of your actions. **Key takeaway:** You created a meaningful gift for your mom, centered on *your* family's history. Stepfather overstepped by treating it as a " family" portrait he's entitled to be in. **You did nothing wrong**. If anything, * he* is the AITA for gaslighting you about a boundary you have every right to set. *(P.S. Your mom's behavior is hurtful, but that's on her—not you. Consider talking to her privately about how this made you feel. You deserve support for your art and your boundaries.)* 💛
